narr: In this video series, we'll explore the English for Engineering I course covering weeks 1 to 4.
This course focuses on fundamental grammar structures and applies them to real communicative tasks in engineering contexts.

data.heading: Course Overview
bullets: Present simple, past simple, present perfect
Quantifiers and relative clauses
Real communicative tasks for engineering contexts

narr: The course covers essential grammar structures including the present simple, past simple, present perfect, quantifiers and relative clauses.
These are applied to practical tasks such as introducing yourself, describing routines and past events, and writing simple definitions.

data.heading: Learning Objectives
bullets: Develop general English proficiency
Academic communication skills
Preparation for engineering coursework in English

narr: By the end of this course, students should have the general English proficiency and academic communication skills needed to follow their engineering coursework in English.

rows.text: Mandatory, Bachelor of Science, all tracks

narr: Let's examine the module information for this course.
The course is English for Engineering I, offered in the Fall semester of 2026-2027.
It's a mandatory module for all Bachelor of Science tracks, worth 4 ECTS credits.
The total workload is 120 hours, with 60 classroom hours and 60 hours of independent study.
The course is coordinated by Ella Tsoy and Florence Dujarric from the Faculty of Energy Engineering.
There are no prerequisites or co-requisites required for this course.

rows.text: Introductions, listening, oral expression: introducing yourself, your studies and your interests; diagnostic test; grammar – tenses; listening to a TED Talk; interactive oral expression
Semester planning, grammar and oral expression: feedback on the diagnostic test; grammar – tenses; listening; interactive oral expression
Numbers and everyday quantification: listening; numbers – practice; grammar – quantifiers; reading comprehension
Reading and writing about movement: grammar – prepositions; reading comprehension – movement and change; written expression

narr: The course is structured over four weeks with specific topics and source materials for each week.
In week 1, students focus on introductions, listening, and oral expression, with materials including lecture notes and grammar worksheets.
Week 2 covers semester planning, grammar review, and oral expression with additional grammar materials.
Week 3 introduces numbers and quantifiers with practice materials and reading comprehension exercises.
Week 4 focuses on reading and writing about movement with prepositions and comprehension exercises.

rows.text: Paper-based reading, writing and listening test

narr: The course assessment consists of five graded components as outlined in the syllabus.
The midterm exam carries 30% weight and focuses on reading and writing tasks.
Test 1 and Test 2 each contribute 10% to the final grade, both being paper-based writing tasks.
Quizzes account for 20% of the grade, with each quiz taking 20 minutes.
The final exam, also worth 30%, includes reading, writing, and listening components.

data.heading: Grading Scale
bullets: 90–100 points = A (Excellent)
75–89 points = B (Good)
60–74 points = C (Satisfactory)
0–59 points = D (Poor)

narr: The grading scale for this course is straightforward, with four performance levels.
Scores from 90 to 100 receive an A for excellent performance.
Scores between 75 and 89 earn a B for good performance.
Scores from 60 to 74 receive a C for satisfactory performance.
Scores below 60 result in a D for poor performance.

data.heading: Attendance and Academic Integrity
bullets: Minimum 75% attendance required to take final exam
Missing 25% or more excludes from final exam
Zero-tolerance policy on plagiarism
AI-assisted work must be cited as a source

narr: The course has strict attendance requirements and academic integrity policies.
Students must attend at least 75% of class meetings to be allowed to take the final exam.
Missing 25% or more of classes excludes a student from the final examination.
The syllabus has a zero-tolerance policy on plagiarism, with penalties ranging from zero on an assignment to automatic failure.
Any AI-assisted work must be properly cited as a source.

narr: Now let's dive into week 1 of the course, which focuses on introductions and the present simple tense with frequency adverbs.

data.heading: Grammar Catalogue for Week 1
bullets: Present simple for routines and habits
Position of frequency adverbs
Diagnostic test and TED Talk listening

narr: Week 1 reviews the present simple for routines and habits and the position of frequency adverbs.
The rules are based on the lecture materials and grammar worksheets for this week.

data.heading: Use of the Present Simple
bullets: Habits and routines (I play tennis every week)
Things that are always true (Sleep is really important for health)
Things we do every day/week/year
Generally true or always happen

narr: The present simple tense has several key uses in English.
We use it to talk about habits and routines, such as playing tennis every week.
It's also used for stating things that are always true, like the importance of sleep for health.
Additionally, we use the present simple for things we do regularly every day, week, or year.
Finally, it's used for things that are generally true or always happen.

data.heading: Form of the Present Simple
bullets: Formed with the infinitive of the verb
Negative sentences: add 'don't' before the verb
Questions: add 'do' before the verb

narr: The form of the present simple is straightforward.
We use the infinitive form of the verb for positive statements.
For negative sentences, we add 'don't' before the verb.
To form questions, we add 'do' before the verb.
